subject: The Slow Garden, issue 41: overwintering dahlias
body:
Hello again, gardeners.

This week the first frost finally arrived, which means the dahlias have to come out of the ground. If you grow them in a cold climate, the routine is simple. Cut the stalks back to about a hand's width once the blackened foliage has collapsed, lift the clumps gently with a fork, and let them dry on newspaper in a shed for a few days. Shake off the loose soil but do not wash the tubers.

Store them in a box of barely damp wood shavings somewhere cool and frost free. Check them once a month and bin anything that has gone soft.

Also in this issue: a short profile of a seed library in a small town hall, three cheap ways to protect young fruit trees from wind, and the reader photo of the week, a surprisingly good cabbage.

Next week we will talk about bare-root roses and why November is the best month to order them.

Until then, keep your hands in the soil.

subject: Build Notes #112: shipping small things
body:
Hi friends,

Three things I learned this fortnight while shipping a tiny side project.

1. Write the changelog before the code. When I describe the change in one sentence for users, half my scope disappears. Two features went from a week of work to an afternoon.

2. Reply to every email you get about the product, even the grumpy ones. You asked how I keep up: I set aside twenty minutes after lunch. Last week a reader wrote to say my export button was confusing, and the fix took ten minutes. That is the best return on time I know of.

3. Do not rebuild your login page in the first month. Someone in the community forum asked about this and the answer from nearly everybody was the same: use the boring default and get back to the actual product.

Reader question of the week: "How do you decide what to cut?" My answer is a list on a sticky note with three columns: needed now, needed soon, and someday. If something sits in the last column for two months it gets deleted without ceremony.

Links I enjoyed: a long essay on small software businesses, a talk on writing fast tests, and a spreadsheet template for tracking experiments.

If this was useful, forward it to one person who builds things. See you in two weeks.

Maya

A longer thought, for those who made it this far. I used to believe that shipping fast meant cutting corners. After two years of doing this in the evenings, I think it is the reverse: the only way to ship often is to make each piece so small that there are no corners left to cut. A tiny change that is carefully tested and clearly described beats a big release that nobody quite trusts. When I look back at the projects that went well, they all had one thing in common, which was a short feedback loop with real users. Five people using something every day taught me more than five hundred who signed up and never came back. I also keep a running list of things I decided not to build, and rereading it every month is oddly satisfying. Several items on it have been requested by readers, and each time I have asked what problem they were really trying to solve, the answer turned out to be simpler than the feature.

subject: Night Sky Notes: what to look for in November
body:
This month the evenings are long and the skies are generally crisp, so let's make the most of them.

Planets: Jupiter rises in the early evening and dominates the eastern sky for most of the night. Saturn sits low in the south after dusk. Through even a small telescope you will see the moons of Jupiter lined up like tiny pearls.

Meteors: a modest shower peaks around the middle of the month. Expect perhaps ten meteors an hour from a dark site after midnight. The Moon will be thin, which helps.

Deep sky target: the great spiral galaxy in Andromeda is high overhead at about nine o'clock. Look for a faint smudge, then use binoculars to see it elongate.

Beginner tip: let your eyes adapt for twenty minutes and use a red torch so you do not ruin your night vision.

Clear skies,
The Night Sky Notes team

subject: Notes on Typography: the case for generous line height
body:
Welcome back.

This week's note is about line height, the most underrated setting on the page. If your text feels cramped, the usual culprit is a line height that is too tight. For body text, a value between 1.4 and 1.6 times the font size is a safe starting point. Long measures need more space, short ones need less.

Three quick experiments to try on your own website: increase line height by a tenth, increase paragraph spacing slightly, and reduce the line length to about sixty-five characters. Compare before and after on a phone.

A reader asked whether serif or sans-serif is easier to read on screens. The honest answer is that it matters far less than size, contrast and spacing.

subject: Policy Brief: how the proposed tax brackets would reshape take-home pay
body:
This week's Policy Brief looks at the government's proposal to restructure income tax brackets.

What is proposed: three of the five brackets would be merged, the lowest threshold would rise modestly, and a new top rate would apply above a high income level. Supporters say the plan simplifies the system. Critics argue it benefits middle earners less than headline figures suggest.

What the modelling says: independent economists estimate that the largest percentage gain goes to households in the middle of the distribution, while those at the very top see a larger dollar gain. Different assumptions about wage growth change the picture, so we show three scenarios side by side.

What happens next: the bill goes to committee next month, and amendments are expected. We will track them.

Further reading: a primer on marginal versus average rates, a glossary of fiscal terms, and a short explainer on bracket creep.

This is general public-policy analysis and does not describe any individual's circumstances.

For context, here is a short history of how the brackets arrived at their current shape. Progressive systems were introduced in stages over the last century, and most countries have adjusted thresholds every few years in response to inflation and political pressure. The last major simplification was fifteen years ago and reduced the number of rates from seven to five. Economists disagree about how much that mattered to behaviour; some studies find little change in hours worked, while others point to shifts in how high earners structure their pay. We include links to four of the most-cited papers and a summary of what each does and does not show. A reminder that our briefs aim to describe options, not to recommend them. We will cover the committee hearings in next week's edition, and we are keeping a running glossary of the terms that come up most often.

subject: Research Roundup: new trials in cardiology and diabetes
body:
Research Roundup, a plain-language summary of what is new in published medical research.

Cardiology: a large multi-centre randomised trial reported that a once-daily combination pill reduced major cardiovascular events compared with usual care over three years. The authors note that the effect was strongest in people over sixty-five. Limitations include a mostly urban study population.

Diabetes: researchers found that continuous glucose monitoring helped adults with type 2 diabetes who do not use insulin to lower average blood sugar over six months. The effect shrank after the device was removed.

Methods corner: what a confidence interval actually tells you, in two paragraphs and one diagram.

Policy: a journal announced stricter rules on trial pre-registration.

All items summarise peer-reviewed publications, with links to the original papers. Nothing here is advice for any individual patient. Speak to a clinician about your own situation.

Also this month: a plain-language guide to reading a clinical trial abstract. Start with the population, because results in one group do not always carry over to another. Look at the comparison arm: usual care, a placebo or another treatment? Check whether the main outcome was decided in advance, and whether the paper reports absolute as well as relative risk. A fifty percent reduction sounds dramatic until you learn that it means going from two cases in a thousand to one. Finally, look at who funded the study and whether the authors declared any competing interests. None of these checks proves anything on its own, but together they make you a more careful reader. We have also added a glossary of fifty terms to our website, with short examples. As always, the digest summarises published literature for a general audience and is not a substitute for professional advice.

body:
Orbit has published a security advisory affecting the command-line tool.

Summary: versions 2.8.0 through 2.8.2 do not properly sanitise file names when unpacking archives. A crafted archive could write files outside the target directory.

Severity: moderate. There is no known exploitation in the wild.

What to do: update to 2.8.3 using your package manager or download it from the releases page. As a workaround, avoid unpacking archives from untrusted sources.
